newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germans launch Berlin Holocaust museum proposal.
newsitem.headline: Germans launch Berlin Holocaust museum proposal.

text.p: A group of prominent German academics and journalists launched a proposal on Friday to build a German Holocaust museum in Berlin, but they admitted it could stir up fresh controversy about the country's Nazi past.

Members of a panel of museum supporters conceded it was almost inevitable the plans for a Holocaust museum would draw Germans into a row similar to the one that has raged for years over a proposed memorial for murdered European Jews.

"This is perhaps the most important period in our history," Lea Rosh, a supporter of the museum, told a news conference. "It is not a coincidence that has not been presented in a proper form yet. This is typical for us (as Germans)."
Rosh, a popular German talk show host, said tensions had already surfaced over whether to house the planned museum in an existing building or to construct a new one.

"This issue is so important that financial crises should not play a role," said Hans-Juergen Haessler, the director of the Institute for Peace and Conflict Research in Hanover and another of the museum's supporters.
Germany still has no official memorial or museum to mark the atrocities of the Nazi era over 50 years after the end of World War Two.
Panelists noted that when the Holocaust Memorial Museum opened in Washington in 1990 several newspapers asked why the land of the Holocaust perpetrators still lacked one.
Proponents hope the foundations will be laid by the year 2000, despite many logistical problems still to be overcome.
They said the museum would focus in particular on support for the Nazis from elite groups such as doctors and judges, and would examine what led to Adolf Hitler's rise.

The planned museum would also contain a international research centre on Germany's fascist history and the development of neo-Nazi movements after the war and would be the country's first dedicated purely to Holocaust issues.

The panelists said they had already begun compiling relevant documents and objects for display in the museum and suggested that federal and state governments, along with private donors and industry, subsidise the project.
The discussion came on the heels of a U.S. congressman's attack this week of the Museum of Contemporary History in Bonn, accusing its directors of ignoring Germany's past before 1945.
Germany has long been embroiled in a debate over how to present accurately the story of its Nazi past -- a sometimes bitter exchange which shows no signs of letting up.

In the immediate post-war years West Germany pushed aside Holocaust issues to focus on developing economic and social stability, while former East Germany buried the persecution of the Jews between 1933 and 1945 under Communist ideology.

Calls for a comprehensive documentation of those years intensified during the 1980s and 1990s, culminating in the demand for memorials for groups victimised by the Nazis and a central museum which would focus on the Holocaust.
"I know from my experience with the memorial debate that we need to be pragmatic and proceed step by step, taking each issue as it comes," said Rosh, who proposed the memorial.
Panel members insisted on the need for a museum focused entirely on the Holocaust, saying the mountains of scholarship produced on the subject each year do not reach average Germans.
"We produce huge volumes on this history, but who reads them?" said military historian Manfred Messerschmidt.

"It is especially important to build a museum for young people," Messerschmidt added. "When this happens, then maybe we could finally begin to have a peaceful discussion on this topic and not attack each other."
